title: Scarborough education centre in desperate need of funding
article: Corey Aaron Armstrong wanted to be a pastry chef.
Late last month, Maryann Poulos got a phone message slip about Armstrong at CARES, the alternative-education centre she runs in Scarborough Village. "Court issues," it said. "Please call his mom."
It was nothing new for Poulos. "That is our client group, they're in and out of jail," she said in an interview.

In April, Armstrong, 21, started classes at CARES preparing for a GED - General Educational Development - exam that would give him a high school diploma. He dropped out, but both he and his mother had called Poulos in June.
"I knew he wanted to come back," she said.
Later that day, though, Armstrong was dead - shot in a Lindsay, ON, house during a gun fight with police that is still under investigation.

Sad as that was, the young Scarborough man was not the first former or current student Poulos had seen lost to violence. She has averaged about one a year since CARES dropped its original addictions mandate and devoted itself to GED preparation in 2008.
Two years ago, Errol Richards, just 19, was stabbed and died just outside the agency's doors on Eglinton Avenue west of Markham Road.

All but ignored by a provincial government who grants the GED diploma but refuses to help pay for exam preparation, CARES has gotten hundreds of clients - most with criminal entanglements, almost all on welfare - a high school diploma.
But CARES may have to close, taking with it clients' hopes of one day escaping poverty or a criminal life.
Poulos told Scarborough councillors last week her annual budget is under $100,000, but for the last two years her parents have covered CARES' shortfall in overhead expenses.
"My client group does not count (with the province)," she said.
"We have until the end of the year, that's it."
David Atkinson, 27, training to be a steamfitter, finished his course at CARES two years ago and said he's grateful Poulos "called me out on my potential."
When he got in legal trouble, he said, CARES held his spot. He hasn't gotten into trouble since, and can look forward to high-paying work for gas refineries or hydro, maybe nuclear power plants.
Atkinson said he couldn't have dreamed of this without a diploma, and doesn't think he could have gotten a diploma by going anywhere but CARES.
"That place needs to stay open," he said.

The attraction of a GED is its speed: students at CARES can earn the necessary credits in 12 weeks or so, and start learning two weeks after registering, instead of enrolling for a regular Grade 12 diploma (perhaps after waiting three months to attend) in courses that take them a year or more to complete.

For-profit centres and school boards also offer GED preparation, but volunteers and program graduates at CARES say their classes of not more than 10 offer individual attention, where GED classes at board-run alternative education centres have as many as 50 students.
Last year, the pass rate for CARES students was 85 per cent.

Armstrong, a quiet student who liked to cook for his family and friends, was excited by the prospect of graduating and going to George Brown College for culinary arts, said Shawn Buckmaster, a former CARES graduate who was his volunteer teacher. "He had aspirations to open his own pastry shop."

Buckmaster, who dropped out in Grade 10 and has volunteered at CARES for two years, joined Poulos and Hedy Baker-Graf, a retired teacher and probation officer, last month in speaking to the Scarborough councillors.
They only wanted their help, Poulos said, in asking the province for support.

The city, she argued, pays part of the cost for welfare, or Ontario Works, cases. About 40 per cent don't have their Grade 12, so getting even some of those clients to pass the GED and get off welfare would save the city and province millions, said Poulos.
But Poulos has tried to get the province's help before, with little success.
In 2008, she spoke to Margarett Best, her local MPP, in a quest to get a meeting with then-Education Minister Kathleen Wynne. Best and other local MPPs said she must appeal to Wynne, she recalled.
Poulos said she was eventually told she wouldn't get funds.
"GED, for the ministry of education, is a dirty little secret," she concluded this week.
Neither Best nor Leona Dombrowsky, the current minister, would respond directly to questions about why the province is unwilling to pay for GED preparation.
Gary Wheeler, a spokesperson for Dombrowsky, sent a written statement stating, "GED preparation services are not regulated in Ontario and are not eligible to receive funding from the province."
Municipalities, the statement added, "may provide subsidies and would be able to provide details."
Yesterday, Wheeler added funding GED preparation would require changes to the province's Education Act and regulations, "and there are no plans to do so at this time."

Rob Foote, Best's senior communication advisor, said the MPP helped Poulos by arranging contacts at another ministry and writing a letter of support in 2008 when Poulos wanted to develop proposals for pre-apprenticeship programs at CARES.
Best "in the past has been an advocate of the organization" he said.
CARES has supporters in Glenn De Baeremaeker, its local councillor, and Gary Crawford, councillor for an adjacent ward, both of which have said they want to help bring its requests to the province.

In CARES, the young clientele "has a peer group of people they trust and believe in," De Baeremaeker said this week, but added the city can do little for the centre, other than perhaps offering some money - not much - it has for retraining Ontario Works recipients.
Putting pressure on the province to listen seems "a faint hope," he said.
David Smith, the local public school trustee, has also visited CARES and met volunteers who graduated and returned to help other students.

"I commend them for their effort, care and passion they have demonstrated in helping those that knock on the door of CARES for the guiding direction," Smith said in a statement Wednesday, calling on the province and city to join in partnership with CARES "to continue to be a good source of producing more graduates and allow these citizens to be valuable contributors to our local economy and beyond."
CARES has not been the only Scarborough agency handicapped by a lack of GED funding.

Second Base Youth Shelter considers GED preparation a vital program, especially for at-risk youth, but without private donations it could not offer GED instruction to its clients, said Marika Goode, acting executive director.
If the province offered support, she said, the shelter could host GED prep five days a week instead of three, and that would be wonderful, she said.
"This is one program that we really don't want to let go," Goode said, describing the impact on students' lives when they pass the exam as huge.
"It's profound."
